DearFlow middleware, explained

A visual guide to what happens before and after the model
5 October 2026

The important idea

  • This report follows the simplified DearFlow CLI in /Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow. It uses your real ilmu-mini-v3.3 runs, saved before/after snapshots, source code and screenshots of your authenticated LangSmith project.

  • All 14 middleware are documented. Each has a purpose, trigger, concrete before/after example and a clear statement of whether it changes the model request, a tool response, graph state or the route through the agent.

  • A turn is one user request until DearFlow stops. One turn may contain several model calls, tool calls and subagent calls. A middleware span is one small recorded operation inside that turn.

  • Every enabled middleware can run without changing a message. A guard activates only when its condition is met. Title changes a label; memory saving is a side effect; neither rewrites the answer.

  • The latest memory learn-and-recall pair passed locally and matched LangSmith snapshots, parent relationships and turn token totals. Older failing memory runs remain failures and are included to explain the fix.

  • The original ten-scenario suite exercised all 14 middleware with real model calls. Some guard tests deliberately seed history or force a tool choice. Those fixtures are identified, and the older suite did not complete the same automated remote comparison.

How to read this report

  • Start with How a turn flows, then the turn examples. Read a middleware entry when you want to understand a particular change. Search the HTML glossary for any unfamiliar field.

  • In LangSmith, open the DearFlow root run, expand the tree and select middleware.<Class>.<hook>. The prefix middleware. identifies the custom before/after capture. The similar unprefixed span is the framework operation around it.

  • For a model wrapper compare Input → before.value with Output → calls[0].request.value. The request is what that wrapper passes onward; later wrappers may still change it. The innermost ChatOpenAI Input shows the final provider-facing message list; tool definitions and model settings are also represented in invocation parameters.

  • To inspect the return path compare Output → calls[0].response.value with Output → result.value. For before/after hooks compare Input → before.value with Output → state_update.value; the update is a patch, not the complete new state.

  • For tool wrappers compare the requested tool and arguments with the handler response and final result. After a tool returns, its result becomes a message available on the next model call.

  • Open Attributes to see Tags, Metadata and Runtime. These describe the run; they are not automatically part of the prompt. Use the glossary to distinguish them from message usage_metadata and tool receipt metadata.

  • Screenshots show selected fields, not every line of a large payload. Exact excerpts, run links and the companion evidence files let you inspect the rest. Markdown rendering can display escaped tags as ordinary tags; compare JSON values when checking exact escaping.

What changes versus what merely describes a run

The model sees text in system_message/messages and tool schemas. LangSmith Metadata is the label on the recording. A field called metadata inside an AI or tool message is a different object. The report names the location of each field, because identical words such as id, status and run_id can refer to different things.

One user turn can contain many model calls

  • A user turn starts when you submit one request and ends when DearFlow gives its final answer or asks a clarification question. Inside that turn, the model can request tools, read their results, and call the model again. LangSmith shows this work as a parent trace with child runs. A middleware hook is a place where extra code runs before or after part of that work; it is not another user message.

  • The verified 03:01 full-flow turn contains seven lead-model calls and four subagent-model calls. The two subagents each call current_time and then write a final report. Their work can overlap; the rows below use recorded span-start order, not a claim that parallel subagent work happened sequentially.

  • Before each lead call, the same wrappers run again. Sanitization and PII produce a fresh outgoing copy; the todo wrapper supplies its instruction block; the receipt ledger grows as tool results arrive. Date and memory preparation normally run once at the start of the user turn. After each model call, the guards inspect its generated tool calls before execution. The final title and memory queue hooks run after the user turn finishes.

  • The lead’s seven calls use 34,051 tokens; subagents use 3,277; the root-turn total is 37,328. Reading all wrapper spans as separate model calls would multiply-count the same work. Use real LLM runs and usage_metadata, not the count of middleware spans. Separate memory extraction is outside this root turn.

Memory: what failed, what changed, what now passes

  • At 02:37 the assistant said it would remember green notebooks and concise bullets, but the first extractor output had malformed JSON. The saved verification review documents two content values missing opening quotes. No facts were saved, so the following full-flow turn had nothing to inject. Later demo instructions were sometimes saved as lasting facts, exposing a separate quality limitation.

  • The first repair added one bounded retry and clarified that temporary tool/demo instructions should not become lasting memory. The 03:01 retry still left memory empty after learning. The saved run records show that behavior failure alongside successful remote trace verification; an export check cannot certify the meaning of the model output.

  • The current extractor requests a validated MemoryFacts tool schema: a facts list whose entries contain nonempty content, a recognized category and confidence from 0 to 1. Facts below the configured 0.7 threshold are dropped. If output is malformed, one retry is allowed. This schema helps enforce shape; it does not prove that extracted facts are true or useful.

  • The 03:30 learning turn saved both expected preferences on its first extraction attempt. A separate new thread then asked for the preferences without providing the answers. Its before_agent snapshot contains both saved facts in <memory>, and its final answer correctly recalls both. The two chat turns and two extraction calls total 7,502 tokens: 3,092 + 626 + 3,146 + 638.

  • All 36 custom middleware snapshots across that pair matched LangSmith, with matching parent relationships and root-turn usage. The extraction diagnostic records show one completed MemoryFacts call for each turn. A duplicate paraphrase of the green-notebook fact remains after recall; this passing smoke test does not demonstrate general memory accuracy, semantic deduplication, or every provider’s behavior.

What these demonstrations prove—and what they leave open

  • All 14 middleware classes appear in the original broad run set. That is coverage of the components, not proof that every optional branch ran. Some hooks legitimately make no change. The detailed component pages distinguish observed examples from additional behavior established by the current code.

  • The long-history, damaged-history, repeated-call, delegation-cap and pending-todo cases use explicit fixtures. The continuation calls are real provider calls, but their starting histories or tool-choice constraints are deliberately constructed. Threshold overrides are identified beside each scenario so they are not confused with normal settings.

  • Historical runs retain their historical status. The original broad suite has eight passing local scenarios and two memory failures; its old remote readback verifier failed. The later 03:01 pair has exact remote matches but still failed memory behavior. The 03:30 memory pair passes both behavior and remote checks. The report combines these evidence sets rather than claiming a single all-branches successful run.

  • Middleware is control and context management, not a truth guarantee. The older time examples contained incorrect weekday/date prose even though current_time returned a correct timestamp, and receipt labels can be misinterpreted across lead and subagent ledgers. A receipt confirms a call happened; a todo marked completed records a model-maintained status; a schema validates structure. Important factual claims still need checking against the actual tool result.

How a turn flows

Start the turn

DynamicContext adds the date; Memory adds saved user facts if available. The state holds messages and working fields such as todos.

Prepare the next model request

Summarization can shorten old history. Todo can add a reminder. Wrappers add receipts, sanitize user text, repair tool history, warn about budget or loops, add planning instructions and mask PII.

Call the model

The model receives the assembled system message, messages and tool definitions. It returns text, requested tool calls and token usage. A requested tool call is not yet an executed action.

Apply response guards

Clarification, Todo, LoopDetection, TokenBudget and SubagentLimit inspect the returned message in reverse middleware order. They may preserve it, add a warning, remove tool calls or change the next step.

Execute tools or finish

If tools remain, their wrappers handle errors, clarification formatting and execution receipts. The loop returns to another model call. Otherwise Title labels the thread and Memory queues extraction for later turns.

scope

Simplified DearFlow repository, not the larger deer-flow monorepo.

main_point

A user turn can contain several model calls and tool calls. Middleware hooks act at different stages; some change outgoing model input, others change generated tool calls, tool results, application state or routing. They do not all rewrite every message.

evidence_boundary

The custom snapshot child spans show immediate middleware boundaries. before → calls[0].request proves request edits; calls[0].response → result proves response edits; node state_update is only a patch, not the complete resulting state.

run_version_note

02:37 broad suite is historical: local snapshot evidence exists but its old verifier reported not verified. 03:01 full flow has exact remote payload/parent/token verification and historical memory failures. 03:30 structured-memory smoke run passed remote verification. No single historical run proves every possible branch of every middleware.

async_note

Methods with leading a (abefore_agent, awrap_model_call, etc.) are asynchronous equivalents, not additional middleware.

all_enabled_does_not_mean_all_mutated

Some guard hooks returned null because conditions were not met. Memory after_agent can return null while still queuing a side effect.

Subagent scope

explanation

Subagents start a fresh context with the task prompt and filtered tools, and inherit only this smaller middleware set. They do not automatically receive the lead conversation, date, long-term memory, summaries, titles or todo plan. Their token usage still contributes to the shared user-turn budget.

All middleware, one by one

01ToolReceiptMiddleware

Why add a receipt to additional_kwargs? See the before/after explanation.

Keeps an execution record so the model can point to tools that actually ran. A receipt says what ran and whether it succeeded; it does not prove an answer is correct.

wrap_model_callwrap_tool_call

See Figure 4: Receipts: the model receives an execution record →

Before the model

Appends a hidden receipt ledger to the model request when receipts exist. In the current demo render_mode is always. The other mode, delegation_only, waits until a subagent result is present in the current turn.

After the model

When the wrapped model returns, stamps the exact ledger shown into the AI message as dearflow_tool_receipt_ledger. It does not rewrite the model’s answer text.

Around tools

After each tool finishes, stamps dearflow_tool_receipt into its ToolMessage, including errors returned by inner middleware. The receipt layer is outermost so it sees the final tool result.

What it affects

Request-only ledger text; metadata attached to real tool and assistant messages.

When nothing changes

No ledger text is added if there are no receipts. A reply can still carry an empty stamped ledger [].

Limits and cautions

  • Receipt ids such as r1 are local to the ledger shown to that agent; a subagent’s r1 need not be the lead agent’s r1.

  • Hashes are compact fingerprints, not full tool arguments or outputs.

  • A citation resolving to a successful receipt confirms execution, not correctness or user acceptance.

Fields and markers to recognise

## Tool receipts (execution record)

The model-visible list of executed tools.

[r1]

A short local label for one displayed receipt.

dearflow_tool_receipt

Structured receipt attached to a tool result.

dearflow_tool_receipt_ledger

Exact receipt list shown when the assistant wrote that answer.

02InputSanitizationMiddleware

Makes real user text visibly separate from application instructions. Reserved tags typed by the user are escaped so they cannot look identical to trusted reminder tags.

wrap_model_call

See Figure 1: Input sanitization: a clear boundary around user text →

See Figure 16: Attributes: labels for identifying a middleware span →

See Figure 17: Attributes: graph position and software versions →

Before the model

Frames every real user text message, including older user messages, in BEGIN/END markers. Changes reserved tags such as <system> to &lt;system&gt;. It copies the model-bound messages and leaves the saved conversation unchanged.

After the model

No after-model transformation. The model’s answer passes back unchanged.

Around tools

No tool hook.

What it affects

Only the outgoing model-request copy of genuine user messages; not system prompt or hidden middleware messages.

When nothing changes

Empty text is unchanged; already framed messages are not repeatedly wrapped. Non-text blocks are preserved.

Limits and cautions

  • This is framing and tag neutralization, not a guarantee that a model cannot follow malicious text.

  • It does not remove all markup or validate facts.

Fields and markers to recognise

--- BEGIN USER INPUT ---

Start of the user-provided text boundary.

--- END USER INPUT ---

End of that boundary.

&lt; and &gt;

Escaped < and > characters, so a reserved tag is treated as text.

03DanglingToolCallMiddleware

Makes history acceptable to providers that require each tool call to have a matching result. Cancelled runs or shortened history can leave unmatched calls/results.

wrap_model_call

See Figure 6: History repair: an interrupted call gets a matching reply →

Before the model

In a request copy, places each matching result after its call, inserts an error placeholder for a call with no result, and leaves out orphan results that have no matching call. It normalizes missing ids, names, and invalid argument shapes when needed.

After the model

No after-model transformation.

Around tools

Does not execute or re-execute a missing tool. A placeholder explicitly says that no result was obtained.

What it affects

Model-request copy only; the original checkpoint still records what actually happened.

When nothing changes

A correctly paired history passes through unchanged.

Limits and cautions

  • The demo deliberately seeded the damaged history; the continuation and fresh current_time call were real.

  • Repair means structurally valid history, not recovery of the missing external result.

Fields and markers to recognise

[Tool call was interrupted and did not return a result.]

A model-visible missing-result placeholder, with status=error.

seed_interrupted_time / seed_orphan_call

Explicit fixture call ids, not new executions.

04ToolErrorHandlingMiddleware

Lets the agent continue after an ordinary tool failure instead of crashing the whole user turn.

wrap_tool_call

See Figure 5: Tool errors: an exception becomes a model-readable result →

Before the model

No direct model-request edit. A recovered error becomes a ToolMessage in history and is visible to the next model call.

After the model

No edit to the model’s answer itself.

Around tools

Catches ordinary exceptions from the inner tool handler and returns status=error with the tool name and failure text. LangGraph control-flow exceptions are re-raised.

What it affects

Tool response; later it becomes part of the model’s input history.

When nothing changes

Successful tool results pass through unchanged.

Limits and cautions

  • The demo proves recovery from calculator division by zero; it does not prove every possible external tool failure.

  • Recovery does not make the failed operation succeed.

Fields and markers to recognise

status=error

The tool failed, but the failure was represented as data the model can read.

error_type

Snapshot record of the inner exception class, separate from the recovered result.

05DynamicContextMiddleware

Gives the model today’s date without changing the stable base system prompt.

before_agent

See Figure 2: Dynamic context: the date becomes a hidden message →

Before the model

Adds a hidden <current_date> message around the latest user message at the start of a turn, when a date reminder is absent or out of date.

After the model

No after-model edit.

Around tools

No tool hook; it reads the application clock rather than calling the model.

What it affects

Conversation state update, then model input on later calls.

When nothing changes

If the conversation already contains a reminder for the same day, it adds nothing.

Limits and cautions

  • A correct date reminder does not guarantee the model’s prose uses the right weekday. One older time-test answer incorrectly said Friday despite the Monday reminder.

06MemoryMiddleware

Carries useful facts from one conversation into a fresh conversation for the same user.

before_agentafter_agent

See Figure 3: Memory: saved preferences enter a new thread →

See Figure 18: Historical memory failure: the model returned malformed JSON →

Before the model

Loads saved facts and inserts a hidden <memory> message before the user prompt. A digest prevents adding the same text repeatedly.

After the model

After the whole agent turn finishes, queues the latest real user message and final assistant text for background extraction. This hook returns null even when it successfully queued work. Persistence happens later; the demo flushes the queue and checks the file.

Around tools

Tool calls and hidden reminder text are excluded from the extracted exchange.

What it affects

Before: conversation context. After: separate memory queue and store, not an immediate state_update.

When nothing changes

No injection when memory is empty, disabled for injection, or unchanged; no exchange is queued when there is no non-empty real user message.

Limits and cautions

  • Earlier 02:37 and 03:01 learning attempts failed. The later 03:30 smoke test is the passing evidence for current structured MemoryFacts extraction.

  • A model saying “I will remember” is insufficient; saved facts and fresh-thread recall were checked.

  • Memory extraction runs outside the completed turn trace in this demo and its tokens are counted separately.

  • Recall produced a paraphrase duplicate of the green-notebook preference in stored memory, so this test is not proof of semantic deduplication.

Fields and markers to recognise

<memory>

Saved context supplied to the model.

[preference]

Fact category: a user preference.

MemoryFacts

The validated tool schema used by the separate extraction call, not an application action tool.

confidence=0.9

Extractor’s confidence score; a filtering score, not a measured probability of truth.

07RedactingSummarizationMiddleware

Keeps long conversations within a manageable context size while retaining a concise account of earlier work.

before_model

See Figure 7: Summarization: replace older messages with a summary →

Before the model

When estimated message tokens reach the trigger, first redacts personal data in the material sent to a separate summary model. Replaces older messages with the generated summary and retains recent messages. It inherits the ordinary summarization behavior and adds redaction for this otherwise separate model path.

After the model

No direct change to the lead model’s answer. The separate summary model’s output is used as new context before the lead model runs.

Around tools

No tool hook.

What it affects

Conversation state replacement, then shortened model input; an extra model call costs tokens.

When nothing changes

Below the summarization trigger it returns no state update.

Limits and cautions

  • The demonstration used fictional seeded workshop history, an 800-token trigger and a 4-message keep setting. It was not a naturally accumulated long chat.

  • Summaries can lose details; retention counts can be adjusted for valid message boundaries.

  • The separate summary model bypasses the main PII wrapper, which is why this redacting subclass exists.

Fields and markers to recognise

type=remove, id=__remove_all__

Clear the old message list before installing the summary plus retained messages.

Beginning of the replacement summary.

SESSION INTENT / SUMMARY / ARTIFACTS / NEXT STEPS

09SubagentLimitMiddleware

Enforces delegation limits even if the model asks for too many subagents.

after_model

See Figure 8: Delegation guard: reject a fourth task request →

Before the model

No before-model rewrite by this class. The base prompt also tells the model the limits, but that prompt text is built elsewhere.

After the model

Examines the generated task calls, keeps only the allowed number, removes excess calls, and appends a limit note. The same AI message id replaces the original, so dropped calls do not reach the tool runner.

Around tools

The task tool starts permitted subagents; this middleware itself does not create them.

What it affects

Changes structured tool_calls and answer text after the model; limits count from the most recent real user message.

When nothing changes

No task calls, or a response within both concurrent and turn-total caps, produces no update.

Limits and cautions

  • The limit fixture seeded three earlier task calls and lowered max_total to 3. It forced the real continuation model to request task, then verified the extra call was removed.

  • The normal demo configuration allows up to 3 task calls per response and 50 per user turn.

Fields and markers to recognise

[SUBAGENT LIMIT REACHED]

Explains that excess delegation calls were removed.

max_concurrent

Task calls allowed in one model response.

max_total

Task calls allowed during one user turn.

10TokenBudgetMiddleware

Tracks accumulated usage for the current turn and asks the model to wrap up before it spends indefinitely.

wrap_model_callafter_model

See Figure 10: Token budget: stop after the current response crosses the cap →

Before the model

Adds a queued TOKEN BUDGET WARNING to the next request, after tool results. It is not stored in the conversation. The first after_model check sets the warning flag; the next wrapper delivers it.

After the model

At the hard threshold, removes all tool calls from the generated answer, adds a budget-exceeded note, and marks stop_reason=token_capped.

Around tools

Budget counts lead-agent, subagent and middleware model calls tracked inside the run; the same guard is inherited by subagents.

What it affects

Warning: request-only text. Hard stop: replacement AI response plus usage state.

When nothing changes

Below thresholds, or outside a tracked RunService turn, it leaves the messages unchanged.

Limits and cautions

  • The hard cap is checked after a model response, so a single response can overshoot the limit. It is not a provider-side prepaid cutoff.

  • Separate background memory extraction in this demo is outside the root turn budget and is reported separately.

  • The warning demo intentionally used a 0.1% threshold; the stop demo used a 1,000-token cap. These are test overrides, not the normal 200,000-token cap.

Fields and markers to recognise

[TOKEN BUDGET WARNING]

Request to finish soon; it does not itself block tools.

[TOKEN BUDGET EXCEEDED]

Hard-stop explanation attached after the model.

stop_reason=token_capped

Turn was stopped by the token guard.

11LoopDetectionMiddleware

Detects when the model keeps requesting the same set of tools with the same arguments.

wrap_model_callafter_model

See Figure 9: Loop guard: stop repeating the same tool call →

Before the model

At the configured warning count, appends a LOOP DETECTED warning to the request. It compares tool names and arguments, ignoring generated call ids and call order.

After the model

At the hard limit, removes tool calls, adds a FORCED STOP note, and records stop_reason=loop_capped.

Around tools

The repeated call that crosses the hard limit never executes.

What it affects

Warning: request-only message. Stop: replacement AI message and usage state.

When nothing changes

Different tool arguments or a nonrepeating sequence do not trigger it. Counting resets at a real user-turn boundary.

Limits and cautions

  • The fixture starts with three seeded identical successful calls and forces calculator as the real model’s tool choice. It proves guard behavior, not that the model naturally entered this loop.

  • Current thresholds are warn after 3 repeats, stop at 5, examining at most the latest 20 call sets.

Fields and markers to recognise

[LOOP DETECTED]

Soft warning to stop repeating and use existing results.

[FORCED STOP]

The hard guard removed another repeated call.

stop_reason=loop_capped

Turn stopped because of repeated tool requests.

12TodoMiddleware

Gives the agent a structured todo list and reminds it not to finish while planned work is still open.

before_modelwrap_model_callafter_model

See Figure 11: Todo guard: send an unfinished answer back to the model →

Before the model

The inherited wrapper appends a write_todos instruction block to the system message. The before_model hook restores a hidden todo-context reminder if saved todos survive but their original tool call has left visible history.

After the model

If the model produces a final answer with unfinished todos, adds a reminder and jump_to=model for another attempt, at most twice per user turn. It also inherits protection against multiple parallel write_todos calls.

Around tools

The inherited write_todos tool replaces the todos list in state and emits a ToolMessage describing the update.

What it affects

System-message copy, todo state, hidden reminder messages, and graph routing.

When nothing changes

No restoration when todos are already visible; no completion reminder when todos are complete or the model is still making tool calls. Stops reminding after the configured maximum.

Limits and cautions

  • The special reminder fixture seeded a pending todo and forced tool_choice=none. The todo stays pending after two reminders; a passing check proves the bounded guard, not completion of the todo.

  • The ordinary full-flow run did complete all five todos.

  • Todo status is model-maintained bookkeeping, not independent proof the action succeeded.

Fields and markers to recognise

write_todos

Tool used to replace the plan’s list.

pending / in_progress / completed

Not started, underway, and marked finished.

<system_reminder>

Todo reminder text; underscore spelling is intentional in this class.

jump_to=model

Route the graph back to another model call.

## write_todos

You have access to the write_todos tool to help you manage and plan complex objectives.
Use this tool for complex objectives to ensure that you are tracking each necessary step.
This tool is very helpful for planning complex objectives, and for breaking down these larger complex objectives into smaller steps.

It is critical that you mark todos as completed as soon as you are done with a step. Do not batch up multiple steps before marking them as completed.
For simple objectives that only require a few steps, it is better to just complete the objective directly and NOT use this tool.
Writing todos takes time and tokens, use it when it is helpful for managing complex many-step problems! But not for simple few-step requests.

## Important To-Do List Usage Notes to Remember

- The write_todos tool should never be called multiple times in parallel.
- Don't be afraid to revise the To-Do list as you go. New information may reveal new tasks that need to be done, or old tasks that are irrelevant.

## Finishing a task

When you finish all work, write your final answer in the message AFTER your last write_todos call — not in the same turn as that call. Start the final message with the substantive content the user asked for — the data, computation, summary, or analysis. The user wants the result, not confirmation that the work is done.

What this means

Actual appended system-message block from LangChain’s inherited todo wrapper.

13PiiRedactionMiddleware

Replaces detected personal data with stable placeholders before selected external text reaches the model.

wrap_model_callwrap_tool_call

See Figure 14: Privacy boundary, before: the exporter needed to redact →

See Figure 15: Privacy boundary, after: the request is already masked →

Before the model

Redacts each real user message in the outgoing request copy. Saved conversation text remains original. Repeated values map to the same keyed placeholder.

After the model

Does not generically rewrite every AI answer. It acts on incoming user text and selected tool results; separate memory/title/summary code handles their own redaction paths.

Around tools

Redacts results from MCP tools and explicitly configured outside-content tool names before the model reads them. Ordinary local tool outputs are left alone.

What it affects

Request copy and selected tool results. The snapshot exporter also separately redacts logged copies, which is why both screenshots can already look masked.

When nothing changes

No recognized personal data means unchanged text; local nonselected tools are not redacted by this tool hook.

Limits and cautions

  • The live example proves user-email masking, not every detector or external-tool route.

  • Supported detectors include email, recognizable API-key forms, checksummed payment-card numbers and certain phone/national-id formats; it is not universal sensitive-data detection.

  • If redaction raises an ordinary exception the current implementation logs a warning and lets original data pass (fail-open).

  • Do not mistake redaction_applied for whether this middleware ran: that flag belongs to the snapshot exporter.

14ClarificationMiddleware

Turns ask_clarification into a question for the user and ends the current turn until the user replies.

after_modelwrap_tool_call

See Figure 12: Clarification: format a question and choices →

Before the model

No request rewrite. The instruction telling the model when to ask is in the base prompt, built elsewhere.

After the model

If ask_clarification appears beside other tool calls, removes sibling calls before they can run. Its after_model hook is first in reverse hook order.

Around tools

Intercepts ask_clarification, formats the question/options itself, returns a ToolMessage and structured human-input artifact. The real tool handler is not called: handler_calls=0 is expected. return_direct ends the turn without another model response.

What it affects

Generated tool_calls, tool result formatting, and conversation routing.

When nothing changes

Ordinary nonclarification responses pass through. If clarification is disabled or the runtime is noninteractive, it returns a continuation instruction and routes back to model instead.

Limits and cautions

  • The real Tokyo/Sydney example proves interception and a formatted question. It did not generate sibling tool calls, so removal of siblings is documented from code, not claimed as exercised live.

  • The user’s reply starts a new run on the same thread; this is a pause in work, not a background model waiting loop.

Why stamp a message?

A stamp is a small record attached to a message so later code knows where it came from, what it represents or what context was available. additional_kwargs is the message's dictionary of extra named fields. It is separate from its content and from LangSmith run metadata.

ToolReceiptMiddleware adds dearflow_tool_receipt to the existing ToolMessage. The tool has already returned. Its result text and call ID stay the same: no second ToolMessage or second tool execution is created by this stamp.

If the exact key is additional_kwargs.tool_calls, that is a different case: a provider adapter may preserve raw call data there while also exposing the same request as AIMessage.tool_calls. The receipt middleware does not create that provider field. Check the key and call ID before treating repeated data as another execution.

Keeping the record beside its result makes it available in saved conversation checkpoints, without mixing audit fields into the answer text. Code can later check a subagent's receipt citations without another model call. Receipts are optional: the basic tool loop can work without them, but it loses this execution record and citation evidence.

One tool execution, before and after

Illustrative example, not a new live test: the model requests calculator with left=17, right=23 and operation="multiply". It executes once and returns "391.0". These excerpts omit unrelated message fields; the timestamp is illustrative and both hashes match these exact example values.

Before the receipt stamp

{
  "type": "tool",
  "name": "calculator",
  "tool_call_id": "call_calc_1",
  "content": "391.0",
  "status": "success",
  "additional_kwargs": {}
}

After the receipt stamp

{
  "type": "tool",
  "name": "calculator",
  "tool_call_id": "call_calc_1",
  "content": "391.0",
  "status": "success",
  "additional_kwargs": {
    "dearflow_tool_receipt": {
      "tool_call_id": "call_calc_1",
      "tool_name": "calculator",
      "status": "success",
      "args_sha256": "48537ccc0704e73f",
      "output_sha256": "dace464a5645ed3d",
      "output_bytes": 5,
      "created_at": "2026-10-05T00:00:00+00:00"
    }
  }
}

Why each receipt field exists

FieldPurpose
tool_call_idConnects the record to call_calc_1. Repeated uses of the same tool have separate call IDs.
tool_nameNames the tool. The citation checker can reject [r1 calculator] if r1 actually names a different tool.
statusCopies the returned message's success/error status. An error gets a receipt too; a receipt alone does not mean success.
args_sha256First 16 hexadecimal characters of a SHA-256 fingerprint of the arguments serialized as sorted-key JSON. A compact identifier, not another copy of the arguments.
output_sha256The same kind of short fingerprint for the returned content. The receipt contains no copy of the output text.
output_bytesUTF-8 size of that content. "391.0" is 5 bytes. Bytes are not tokens.
created_atUTC time when the middleware stamps the returned result. It is not the call's duration.
id: "r1"Added later when receipts are listed in message order. It is a citation label, not the stable tool_call_id; it is absent from the initial stamp above.

The receipt wrapper sits outside the other tool wrappers. It records the result they return, including an error message produced by error handling or content changed by redaction. The argument fingerprint uses the request seen by this wrapper. DearFlow overwrites its own receipt key rather than accepting a tool-supplied value, while preserving other additional_kwargs fields.

A receipt records a returned call and its reported status. The current citation checker checks the ID, status and optional tool-name anchor; it does not recompute the hashes or validate the answer. These short fingerprints are not encryption, a digital signature or a tamper-proof certificate. A resolved citation does not prove the user's task is complete.

Why stamp the model reply too?

WhenWhat happensWhy
1. Tool returnsStamp the existing ToolMessagedearflow_tool_receipt records this result for later audit and listing.
2. Next model requestAdd a temporary receipt list when enabledA request-only HumanMessage makes the receipt IDs readable to the model.
3. Model repliesStamp the existing AIMessagedearflow_tool_receipt_ledger preserves exactly the numbered receipts offered on that request.
4. Check a helper reportResolve its citations with codeMatch [r1 calculator] against the helper reply's preserved list, not a newly renumbered history.

Why keep another list on the reply? Suppose a reply cites [r2] for the calculator. Later, summarization removes an older r1 message and the surviving calculator receipt becomes r1. Rebuilding the list now would misread the old citation. The reply's stamped ledger freezes the original numbering. It also keeps only the entries that fit in the rendered list.

The hidden ledger message has dearflow_injected: "receipt_ledger" and hide_from_ui: true. Hidden means hidden from the chat display, not from the model. Its content is included in the outgoing request and uses prompt tokens. It is not stored as a new conversation message. The receipt list stamped on the returning AIMessage is application metadata, not another model response.

Shortened model-visible ledger example

## Tool receipts (execution record)
...
- [r1] calculator status=success
  args_sha256=48537ccc0704e73f
  output_sha256=dace464a5645ed3d

The default lead setting is receipts_render_mode: "delegation_only": a normal calculator turn can have a tool receipt without a visible-to-model ledger. The lead renders it when reading a task result in the current turn. With always, receipts are rendered whenever present; enabled subagent receipts use this mode. The list has a 2,000-character budget, dropping older entries when needed. An active render path with no receipts can stamp [] without adding a hidden message.

Why other extra fields exist

FieldAdded byPurpose
dearflow_injectedDearFlow middleware / helpersMarks date, memory, todo, receipt-ledger or loop-warning context as framework-added. Code can distinguish it from a real user message.
hide_from_uiDearFlow middleware / helpersLets DearFlow's normal message display filter internal reminders. It does not prevent model visibility or hide the message from traces.
reminder_dateDynamicContextMiddlewareRemembers which date was injected so the same date reminder need not be added every turn.
memory_digestMemoryMiddlewareFingerprints the injected memory text so unchanged context is not added repeatedly. It is not a memory-save success flag.
subagent_statustask toolPreserves whether the helper completed, failed, timed out or reached its turn limit beside its returned report.
tool_receipts / receipt_verdicttask toolKeeps the helper's receipt list and advisory citation check beside its report. The lead's task call also gets its own separate receipt.
tool_calls / function_callProvider adapter, when presentMay be the raw provider representation of the same requested call also exposed as AIMessage.tool_calls. These are different keys from DearFlow's receipts; duplicate-looking serialization is not proof of duplicate execution.

How to check this in LangSmith

  1. Open middleware.ToolReceiptMiddleware.wrap_tool_call (or its async equivalent). Compare calls[0].response.value with result.value: the same result content and tool_call_id remain, while additional_kwargs.dearflow_tool_receipt appears.
  2. For wrap_model_call, compare before.value with calls[0].request.value for the temporary ledger. Compare calls[0].response.value with result.value for the reply's dearflow_tool_receipt_ledger. A later inner wrapper may still change the forwarded request.
  3. Custom message snapshots allowlist the two DearFlow receipt keys. Other additional_kwargs fields may be missing from that view even when present at runtime. Provider traces and stored messages can show a different selection.
  4. Count actual tool runs and actual LLM runs to detect extra work. A metadata stamp creates neither. A rendered ledger can increase input tokens on an already scheduled model call; it does not schedule another call.

Metadata and keywords

Middleware

A small piece of code around the agent that can add context, repair messages, enforce limits, catch errors or record work. Not every middleware edits the prompt, and not every invocation changes anything.

Turn

One user request and all graph steps needed to answer it. It may include several model calls and tool calls. The report’s separate scenarios are separate turns, often separate test conversations.

Hook

The stage where a middleware is called: before_agent once as a turn begins; before_model before each model step; wrap_model_call around model requests/responses; after_model after a model step; wrap_tool_call around a tool; after_agent as the turn ends.

Request path and return path

Wrapping middleware run in chain order on the way in and unwind in reverse order on the way out. A wrapper’s response boundary is the result from its inner layer. After-model node hooks also execute in reverse middleware order.

No-op

A hook ran but its condition did not apply, so it forwarded unchanged data or returned no state patch. That is expected; it is not a missing middleware.

State versus model request

State is the stored working conversation. A wrapper can change only the copy sent to the model, leaving the checkpoint untouched. Node hook patches can instead change durable state. Inspect the final ChatOpenAI Input for the assembled provider-facing message list; inspect invocation parameters for tool definitions and model settings.

Trace, span and thread

A thread is a conversation; a trace contains one execution; a span is one operation inside that trace. A middleware child span is instrumentation, not necessarily another model call.

Metadata versus message content

Metadata describes the run for filtering, grouping and debugging. It does not automatically become prompt text. Input/output objects can contain actual messages, state patches, diagnostics and control data; inspect their field and boundary before deciding the model saw them.

Checkpoint

A saved version of graph state used to continue or resume a conversation. It differs from long-term user memory, which is extracted into facts and can be injected into a different thread.

<memory>, <system-reminder>, <current_date>, <system_reminder>

Text markers used in framework-injected context. The surrounding text tells the model what the block means. Input sanitization neutralizes reserved tags in real user messages so user text cannot impersonate those injected blocks.

[EMAIL_…], [PHONE_…] and similar placeholders

Stable replacements for detected personal data. They let repeated references remain consistent without sending the original value along that protected path. They are not reversible plaintext shown in the report.

[r1 calculator]

A model’s citation to numbered execution receipt r1, anchored to the calculator tool. It supports matching a statement to a recorded call; it does not prove the statement’s factual correctness.

LangSmith screenshots

Captured from the authenticated LangSmith dashboard. Click any image to inspect it at a larger size.

What the evidence proves

  • This report describes the simplified DearFlow code and the captured 5 October runs, not the larger DeerFlow monorepo.

  • A successful span means its operation finished. It does not by itself prove that memory persisted, a guard changed anything, or a tool result was correct. The before/after assertions provide that evidence.

  • The full-flow retry used 37,328 turn tokens across eleven LLM calls. Background memory extraction is separate; adding parent spans to child spans would double-count usage.

  • The latest memory pair used 6,238 turn tokens plus 1,264 background extraction tokens, or 7,502 combined. Cached input tokens are a subset of input tokens, not an extra chargeable count to add again.

  • PII masking in custom snapshots is distinct from runtime PII middleware. Native LangSmith traces can retain different data. Redaction is not a proof that every trace or field is anonymous.

  • No new provider calls were needed to write this report. Screenshots are read-only captures of existing traces.

Seeing all middleware

Use Tree settings → Show All. A reduced or Most relevant tree may hide wrapping-hook spans. Look for the custom middleware.<Class>.<hook> child and its before/calls/result fields.

/Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow/docs/observability.md:54

Snapshot redaction is separate from runtime PII protection

The snapshot exporter redacts its own saved copies. That can make both sides look masked even when only the runtime middleware changed the true outgoing request. The redaction_applied flag disambiguates this boundary. Custom snapshots do not globally redact native root inputs, all LangSmith traces, the CLI, or saved raw conversations.

/Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow/src/dearflow/observability/snapshots.py:87

PII protection has explicit scope and a fail-open path

Runtime PII middleware protects real-user message copies and selected outside tool results. It does not promise to redact every field or every local tool. If redaction itself raises, current code logs a warning and forwards original data. Summarization has its own analogous redaction path.

/Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow/src/dearflow/middlewares/pii_redaction.py:25

Memory extraction is background work

after_agent queues an exchange and returns no state patch. A timer or demo flush later runs a separate extractor model call. Those calls can be standalone traces and lie outside the turn’s usage registry; count their usage separately when reporting total spend. Stored facts and a fresh-thread recall test prove learning, not a polite “I will remember” reply.

/Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow/src/dearflow/memory/manager.py:15

Token and time double-counting

Count each actual LLM span once. Never add parent aggregate totals, nested wrapper totals, per-model breakdowns, receipt counts and leaf-model totals together. Wrapping durations are inclusive and parallel spans overlap. Provider absence of token data is unknown usage, not proof of a free call.

/Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow/src/dearflow/usage/tracker.py:95

A completed trace is not a correct answer

LangSmith success records execution outcome. It does not independently validate dates, facts, tool choices or accepted task completion. Receipt checks only match citations to execution records.

/Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow/src/dearflow/receipts/verification.py:1

No universal metadata dictionary

This glossary covers the project’s own keys and the installed tracing stack’s relevant fields. Optional provider/runtime fields may differ by SDK version or environment. Unknown fields should be identified from their producing integration rather than guessed.

/Users/johnathanjohnathan/Documents/dearflow/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/langsmith/env/_runtime_env.py:185

Capture boundaries and limits

Snapshots are bounded, allowlisted copies rather than a full execution dump. They retain at most eight forwarded calls per wrapper, depth eight, up to 100 collection entries, 1,000 walked nodes and a configured serialized-character limit. Binary data and nonallowlisted message metadata are omitted. A false truncated flag still does not make this a capture of every possible object field.
